doc.title: Stefon Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2020

title: Love, trust and respect in Blackout; composition as discovery
summary: Asked about instructing bandmates over seventeen years, Harris says the band runs on love, trust and respect and that composition is discovery shaped by divergent perspectives.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Well keeping a group of musicians together for seventeen years is quite an accomplishment. I mean keeping them together for seven days is sometimes impossible. We all do so many things. When you’re working on a tune, perhaps in a rehearsal, and it’s a composition of yours, how comfortable are you with — I’ll use the word “instructing” or “suggesting” to your fellow musicians how to play? Or perhaps what not to play?

That’s another great question. I would tell you as an improviser I think our success is predicated upon three fundamental values. Those values are love, trust, and respect. When we walk into a room to learn a new piece of music we are leading with that. I never tell Terreon what to play on the drums. Never. There’s no need because I’ve done it maybe twice over the course of the past seventeen years, and both times what I suggested was nowhere near the level of what he came up with on his own. And the same is true of Marc and Casey. So really when I’m composing it’s not so much that I own the idea. I think of composition as not really a creative process, it’s really a process of discovery. I spent the majority of my time, like a lot of musicians, working on my ear, working on my ability to perceive possibility. So when I sit it’s not that something’s already in my mind — I find it — oh that’s how that works, oh this will fit there. So I’ve contributed that portion. When I bring it in to the other guys in the band, they’re perceiving other parts of it that I can’t see. And it’s that conglomerate of imagination of intelligence, of informed diverse culture, that creates the magic that is jazz. What we make is so much bigger than what I could do on my own. It’s really only possible if we have divergent perspectives, people who don’t think the same way, people who disagree who come together. Magic lives in between those interesting spaces between disparate ideas.
